data.title: THE PULLMAN STRIKE
data.subtitle: Pullman, Illinois — Spring to Summer, 1894
data.introBody: Spring, 1894. You are a skilled car worker living in the company town of Pullman, Illinois. George Pullman cut your wages again last month — but not your rent. The strike vote is coming, and whatever you decide, the same hand that signs your paycheck holds the keys to your front door.
data.trailFeedOpener: May 1894: the Pullman Arcade Hall is filling up. Men you have worked beside for years are talking low and hard.

events.title: The night of the local ARU vote — late May 1894, inside the Pullman Arcade hall
events.text: The hall is packed and hot. The foreman at your bench pulled you aside this afternoon and made it plain: workers who vote to strike will be noted by name. Your rent ledger is already two weeks behind — the company docked wages again last month without touching the rent. Your wife is three months from her time. Eugene Debs's man is at the front of the room calling the vote. The men around you — men you have worked next to for years — are rising one by one. The ballot is in your hand.

choices.text: You stand. You drop the ballot in the box with the others. Whatever comes next, you came down on this side.
choices.result: The player has chosen to be the kind of person who answers a collective claim even at private cost — not because it is safe, but because standing apart felt like a betrayal of something that mattered more than safety.

choices.text: You stay seated. You slip the ballot into your coat. Your wife's face is in your mind and you cannot move past it.
choices.result: The player has chosen to be the kind of person whose first obligation runs to the people under his own roof — not because solidarity doesn't matter, but because the weight of a particular face made the abstraction impossible to hold.

events.title: The Notice on the Board
events.text: A white slip appears on the shop floor bulletin board. Wages cut another eighteen percent — effective Monday. The rent ledger stays untouched. Men stand reading it in silence, hats in hand.
trivia: George Pullman cut wages in 1894 but refused to lower rents in his company town.
Workers in Pullman paid rent, utilities, and store credit all to the same company that paid their wages.

choices.text: Sign the grievance petition with your neighbors.
choices.result: Forty names go on the paper. The foreman takes note of yours. Your neighbors nod at you in the street that evening.

choices.text: Read it, say nothing, walk back to your bench.
choices.result: You keep your head down. The foreman does not write your name. A quiet choice — but the men around you noticed.

choices.text: Tell a neighbor to think before signing anything.
choices.result: He looks at you a long moment, then walks away. You told yourself it was good advice. It didn't feel that way.

image.artist: Unknown author; 'Pullman Company negative jacket labeled "Fife and Drum Corp"' [1]

events.title: Credit at the Company Store
events.text: Your pay envelope this week is three dollars after deductions. The company store clerk tells you your tab is overdue. Your wife needs flour and lamp oil. The ARU relief fund is taking donations from those who can spare anything.
events.imageSearchQuery: Pullman Palace Car Company store Illinois
trivia: In the Pullman company town, workers' wages were paid and immediately reduced by rent, gas, water, and store charges before the worker received any cash.

choices.text: Pay the tab. Keep credit with the company.
choices.result: The clerk marks you current. Your wife has flour tonight. The relief fund goes without your contribution.

choices.text: Give two dollars to the ARU relief fund.
choices.result: You hand over two dollars you could not really spare. Your wife sees what you did and says nothing. The fund secretary writes your name down.

choices.text: Ask the clerk for an extension. Buy time.
choices.result: The clerk writes it down. You are on the list now — men the housing office watches more closely. You bought a week.

image.searchQuery: Pullman Palace Car Company store Illinois

events.title: The Association Brings In New Men
events.text: The General Managers' Association has hired replacement workers. A delegate from the railroads posts notices: men who return to work will be given their jobs back, no questions asked. The picket line outside the car shops grows thinner each morning.
trivia: The General Managers' Association coordinated the twenty-four Chicago railroads against the ARU boycott, firing union members and hiring replacements to break the strike.

choices.text: Hold the line. Stay off the job.
choices.result: You stand at the gate in the morning cold. Your wife counts the coins left in the jar on the shelf. The men who stayed say your name with something like respect.

choices.text: Report back to the shop floor quietly.
choices.result: The foreman says nothing when you sit down at your bench. Three men you know see you through the window. They do not wave.

choices.text: Wait another week before deciding.
choices.result: You do not cross, but you do not stand either. The week bleeds out, and nothing is resolved by your silence.

image.artist: Unknown author; 'Pullman Company negative jacket labeled "Fife and Drum Corp"' [1]

events.title: The Injunction Posted
events.text: Attorney General Olney has secured a federal injunction. It orders ARU members to stop interfering with mail trains — on penalty of arrest. U.S. marshals are posted at the rail yards. Debs calls it a death sentence for the boycott.
trivia: Richard Olney, a former railroad lawyer serving as U.S. Attorney General, used the Sherman Antitrust Act to obtain a sweeping injunction against the ARU boycott in July 1894.
The injunction made continuing the boycott a federal crime, and Eugene Debs was arrested for contempt of court.

choices.text: Attend the ARU meeting. Hear Debs out.
choices.result: The hall is half the size it was in May. Debs speaks plainly: the government has sided with the railroads. You stay till the end. A marshal outside takes note of who leaves.

choices.text: Stay home. Avoid being seen at union halls.
choices.result: Your name is not on any new list tonight. Your wife says that is the wisest thing you have done in weeks. The injunction tightens around the men who went.

choices.text: Report the meeting's attendees to the housing office.
choices.result: The housing agent thanks you and marks your ledger current. Two neighbors are served eviction papers by the end of the week. You know you did that.

events.title: Federal Troops on the Streets
events.text: President Cleveland has sent federal troops to Chicago over the Illinois governor's protest. Soldiers are posted at the yards. Two men from your block were arrested this morning. The strike is dying — but it is not dead yet.
trivia: President Grover Cleveland ordered federal troops to Chicago in July 1894 over the objection of Illinois Governor Altgeld, who argued the state could handle the situation without federal intervention.
The arrival of federal troops effectively broke the Pullman Strike, which collapsed within days.

choices.text: Bring food to the families of arrested men.
choices.result: You carry a pot of soup down the block. The wife of one arrested man holds your hand at the door for a long moment. You do not say much. Neither does she.

choices.text: Warn your family to stay indoors and lie low.
choices.result: Your children do not go out for two days. Nobody bothers you. Somewhere nearby, other families face the soldiers without help from you.

image.artist: Unknown author; 'Pullman Company negative jacket labeled "Fife and Drum Corp"' [1]

events.title: The Strike Is Broken — What Now
events.text: The ARU is finished. Debs is in jail. The company is issuing new work contracts with a loyalty clause: you must affirm you were never a union agitator to be rehired. Men who held the line longest are being denied contracts entirely. You must decide what you sign — and who you speak for.

choices.text: Sign the loyalty clause. Secure your family's future.
choices.result: Your name is cleared and you return to the shop. The foreman shakes your hand. You recognize two of the men who were denied contracts — you worked next to them for six years. You do not meet their eyes.

choices.text: Refuse the clause. Stand with the blacklisted men.
choices.result: You hand the paper back unsigned. The housing agent is at your door before the week is out. Your wife stands beside you in the front room when he comes. She does not ask you to change your answer.

choices.text: Sign, but quietly give money to a blacklisted family.
choices.result: You get your job back and slip ten dollars under a neighbor's door. It helps them one week. It does not get their father his job back. You tell yourself you did what you could.

image.artist: Unknown author; 'Pullman Company negative jacket labeled "Fife and Drum Corp"' [1]

events.title: Late June 1894 — the federal injunction has been issued and U.S. marshals are posted at the rail yards. A neighbor whose husband is on the picket line comes to your door asking if she can keep her children with you for the day because there is no food in her house and she is going to the relief committee.

text.default: You open the door wide without a word. You are already lean yourself — the company has not rehired the strikers and you have been living on what the ARU relief fund can spare. But she is part of what you chose, and you cannot close the door on that. The children come in. You divide what is in the pot.

variants.text: You open the door wide without a word. You are already lean yourself — the company has not rehired the strikers and you have been living on what the ARU relief fund can spare. But she is part of what you chose, and you cannot close the door on that. The children come in. You divide what is in the pot.

You open the door and look at her face and feel the thing you have been not-feeling for weeks press up under your sternum. You are still employed. Your rent is current. You let the children in and you feed them, and you do not say anything about why your house has food and hers does not, and neither does she, and the silence between you is its own kind of verdict that neither of you pronounces aloud.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Pullman Worker
sages.title: Company-Town Laborer & Tenant
sages.bio: A skilled car finisher who has lived in Pullman since the town opened. He pays rent, water, and gas to the same company that employs him — and has watched each paycheck shrink while the rent ledger stays fixed.
sages.greeting: A man from your finishing crew catches you after the shift bell. His hands are still chalked from the work. He speaks quietly so the foreman cannot hear.
sages.advice: "You know what I cleared last week? Two dollars and eleven cents. After they took the rent and the gas and what I owed the store. Two dollars. My boy needs shoes."

question.question: What was unique about the town of Pullman that made workers especially vulnerable during the strike?
choices: It was located too far from Chicago for workers to find other jobs
The Pullman company owned the workers' homes, stores, and utilities — not just the factory
Workers in Pullman were paid in company scrip instead of U.S. dollars
The town had no schools or churches, so families had no community ties
question.explanation: George Pullman owned everything in the town — the houses, the stores, the water, the gas, and even the church. Workers' wages were paid and then immediately reduced by rent, utilities, and store charges before workers ever held the cash. This gave the company complete leverage over every aspect of workers' lives.
question.teksRef: 8.20(A) — Economic causes and effects of labor conflicts in the Gilded Age

sages.name: Eugene V. Debs
sages.title: President, American Railway Union
sages.bio: Eugene V. Debs founded the American Railway Union in 1893 as an industrial union open to all railroad workers regardless of craft. When the Pullman workers voted to strike, his ARU called a national sympathetic boycott — refusing to handle Pullman cars — that shut down rail lines across twenty-seven states.
sages.greeting: Debs is in Chicago for a meeting of ARU locals. Someone passes word he will speak to any Pullman man who comes to the hall on Wabash Avenue.
sages.advice: "The railroads are one system. We must be one union. Every man who refuses to couple a Pullman car is the boycott. You are the boycott."

question.question: What action did Eugene Debs and the ARU take to support the Pullman strikers that turned a local walkout into a national crisis?
choices: They organized a march on Washington to petition President Cleveland
They called a national sympathetic boycott — ARU members refused to handle any Pullman cars on any railroad
They filed a federal lawsuit against the General Managers' Association
They negotiated directly with George Pullman on behalf of the workers
question.explanation: Debs and the ARU declared a sympathetic boycott: ARU members on railroads nationwide would refuse to handle any train that included Pullman sleeping cars. This transformed a local wage dispute into a system-wide shutdown affecting rail traffic across twenty-seven states and forcing a federal response.
question.teksRef: 8.20(B) — The role of organized labor in Gilded Age industrial conflicts

sages.name: Richard Olney
sages.title: U.S. Attorney General
sages.bio: Richard Olney served as U.S. Attorney General under President Grover Cleveland. Before entering government, he had been a railroad lawyer. In July 1894, Olney obtained a sweeping federal injunction against the ARU boycott, using the Sherman Antitrust Act — a law written to curb corporate monopolies — as the legal weapon that broke the strike and sent Debs to prison.
sages.greeting: A labor lawyer in Chicago passes you a copy of the federal injunction. He reads you the key passage aloud. It is signed by Olney's office.
sages.advice: "The injunction forbids any interference with interstate commerce or the U.S. mail. Debs has been warned. Any man who continues the boycott can be held in contempt — no jury required."

question.question: How did Attorney General Olney use the Sherman Antitrust Act against the ARU — and why was that significant?
choices: He used it to break up the Pullman Palace Car Company as an illegal monopoly
He argued the ARU boycott was an illegal restraint of trade, turning a law meant for corporations into a weapon against labor
He used it to fine individual workers who refused to return to their jobs
He cited it to seize ARU funds and distribute them to replacement workers
question.explanation: The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 was written to break up corporate monopolies. Olney argued that the ARU boycott was itself a 'conspiracy in restraint of trade' under the Act. This turned a law designed to protect workers and consumers from corporate power into the legal instrument that criminalized the strike and exposed Debs to arrest.
question.teksRef: 8.20(C) — Federal power and legal instruments in Gilded Age labor disputes

data.historicalContext: The Pullman Strike of 1894 ended in total defeat for the workers. Federal troops and a sweeping injunction broke the boycott within weeks. The American Railway Union collapsed. Eugene Debs was sentenced to six months in prison for contempt of court. George Pullman never negotiated with his employees. The company town of Pullman continued to operate under the same terms until courts ordered its sale in 1898. Roughly thirty people died in strike-related violence nationwide. The strike's failure demonstrated the willingness of the federal government to side with capital against organized labor — but it also radicalized a generation of workers and pushed Debs toward the socialist movement he would lead for the next three decades.

data.reviewSummary:
In the spring of 1894, workers at the Pullman Palace Car Company in Pullman, Illinois, were living inside a system George Pullman controlled completely. He owned the houses they rented, the stores where they bought food, the water and gas lines into their homes, and the church in the town square. When Pullman cut wages by roughly 25 percent that spring to keep profits steady during a national depression, he refused to reduce rents by a single dollar. Workers who formed a grievance committee and met with management to ask for relief were rejected — and three committee members were laid off shortly afterward. That triggered the strike vote of late May 1894.

Eugene Debs, president of the American Railway Union, turned the local walkout into a national crisis on June 26 by calling a sympathetic boycott: ARU members across the country refused to handle any train that included Pullman sleeping cars. Within days, rail traffic in twenty-seven states was paralyzed. The General Managers' Association — a coordinating bloc of twenty-four Chicago railroads — responded by firing ARU members, hiring replacement workers, and pressing the federal government for intervention.

Attorney General Richard Olney, a former railroad lawyer, obtained a sweeping federal injunction in early July using the Sherman Antitrust Act — a law written to break up corporate monopolies — as the legal weapon against the union, arguing the boycott was an illegal restraint of trade. President Grover Cleveland then ordered federal troops to Chicago over the protest of Illinois Governor Altgeld, who believed the state could manage the situation without federal force. The troops arrived and the boycott collapsed within days.

Debs was arrested for contempt of court, convicted, and sentenced to six months in prison. The ARU dissolved. George Pullman never negotiated with his workers. The company shared blacklists with other railroads, ensuring that strike participants could not find work in the industry again. The strike's defeat showed that in the Gilded Age, federal power — troops, courts, and law — could be mobilized decisively on the side of employers. Debs emerged from prison radicalized, and went on to lead the Socialist Party and run for president five times. The Pullman company town was ordered sold by the courts in 1898.

data.subtitle: Montgomery, Alabama — December 1955 to December 1956
data.introBody: December 1, 1955. Montgomery, Alabama. Rosa Parks refused her seat on a city bus today, and by morning the women on your block will be asking what you mean to do. You are a domestic worker — you walk two miles each way to Mrs. Hartwell's kitchen, you bring home a few dollars a week, and you know every cracked sidewalk between Dexter Avenue and the white neighborhood on the other side of town. The boycott is asking something of you. So is your family. Neither will be satisfied by the same answer.
data.trailFeedOpener: Monday morning, December 5, 1955. The buses run empty past your corner. You lace your shoes.

events.title: Week Three of the Boycott — Thursday morning, your employer meets you at the back door
events.text: Mrs. Hartwell is waiting on the porch when you arrive, feet already aching from the two-mile walk. She speaks quietly, not unkindly. She says she has heard you are walking because of the trouble, and she respects that you have feelings about it, but her husband's brother saw you on Dexter Avenue and has been asking questions — questions that could make things difficult for her family too. She says she can send her husband's car for you each morning. Nobody has to know. She is not demanding. She is asking. And behind her voice is the unspoken fact you both know: if you refuse and the talk keeps coming, she will have no choice but to let you go. You think of your daughter's school shoes, worn through at the toe. You think of the other women you walk with each morning, the ones who check on you at the corner of Mobile Street.

The women on your block walked for 381 days in the cold and the heat, organized a 300-car carpool on goodwill and gas money, and held together long enough for a federal court to say what they always knew: the law had been wrong. You were there. You walked some mornings. You passed the plate and kept moving. The boycott won without requiring much of you, and you let it.

data.title: STAR-SPANGLED TRIAL
data.subtitle: A Young Militiaman in the War of 1812
data.introBody: Summer, 1812. You are a young state militiaman called up to defend your home county. The army feeds you poorly and pays you late. Your worn musket, your empty belly, and your neighbors' eyes on you — these are your real stakes.
data.trailFeedOpener: June 1812: Congress declares war on Britain. Your company musters at the county courthouse.

events.title: Early Campaign — The March Order
events.text: A federal officer rides into camp and reads orders: the militia company is to cross into the next territory and reinforce a position the regulars cannot hold alone. Your captain looks at the ground. Half the men came from the same two townships. The harvest is weeks out. Word has it a British raiding party burned a farm two counties over. The officer says those who refuse will be noted — but the constitutional question is unsettled and he knows it. Your messmate whispers that his wife is alone. The man next to him is already checking his cartridge box.

choices.text: Fall in with those crossing. The line on a map is not the line that matters — the enemy is real and the regulars need bodies.
choices.result: He defines himself as a soldier of the republic first and a neighbor second — a man who can be called somewhere he did not plan to go, by a cause larger than the county he came from.

choices.text: Stand your ground here. You enlisted to protect this region, and that oath has not been satisfied — marching away does not make you a better soldier, only a different one.
choices.result: He defines himself by the specific community that gave him his identity — a man whose loyalty is honest precisely because it has a known shape, and who will not let that shape be redrawn by a distant order.

events.title: A Sailor's Account
events.text: A haggard man in a torn jacket sits by your mess fire. He says the Royal Navy stopped his ship, declared him a British subject, and dragged him aboard a man-of-war for three years. Your messmates listen hard.
trivia: The Royal Navy claimed the right to seize sailors it deemed British subjects, even from American ships.
Thousands of American merchant sailors were impressed into British service before 1812.

choices.text: Share your rations and let him rest by the fire.
choices.result: He eats slowly, says nothing for a long time, then thanks you by name. Word spreads through camp.

choices.text: Hear him out, then move on to your duties.
choices.result: You listen, nod, and return to your post. It sits with you all night.

choices.text: Tell him the army has enough troubles without his.
choices.result: He goes quiet and leaves before dawn. The men who heard you say nothing to your face.

events.title: The War Hawk's Argument
events.text: A congressman in riding clothes stops at your company's camp. He speaks loudly about British arms to hostile Indians, seized trade, and national honor. He wants your captain to confirm the men are eager to fight.
trivia: War Hawks like Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun argued that British interference in trade and support for Indian resistance made war necessary.
Many War Hawks came from western and southern states, not the coastal merchant cities.

choices.text: Stay quiet and let the captain answer.
choices.result: The captain speaks carefully. You watch and say nothing. Later a sergeant nods at you — steadiness counts.

choices.text: Speak up — tell him the men have real grievances.
choices.result: The congressman looks surprised. Several messmates clap you on the shoulder after he rides away.

choices.text: Tell him loudly the men are ready — earn his favor.
choices.result: He presses a coin in your palm and rides off. Two older men in the company look away.

image.artist: Julian Vannerson or Montgomery P. Simons

events.title: Empty Ration Wagon
events.text: The quartermaster's wagon arrives three days late and half empty. Hardtack and salt pork are gone. The men are on short rations and tempers are short. You have a few coins and some dried corn from home.
trivia: American forces in the War of 1812 suffered badly from supply failures — Congress underfunded the army and state militia systems were fragmented.
Militiamen often had to purchase their own food and equipment when official supplies ran short.

choices.text: Spend coins on extra food for the mess.
choices.result: Your messmates eat. Nobody mentions the coins, but nobody forgets either.

choices.text: Keep your coins — you may need them more later.
choices.result: You go hungry with the rest. The coins are still in your pocket, and so is the hunger.

choices.text: Report the shortage to the sergeant and wait.
choices.result: The sergeant shrugs. Word eventually reaches an officer and a resupply is promised — in two days.

image.artist: Clockwise, from top: George Munger, John David Kelly, Anton Otto Fischer, William Emmons, Edward Percy Moran

events.title: The Capital in Flames
events.text: Riders arrive with news: Admiral Cockburn's forces have taken Washington. The Capitol and the President's House are burning. Your captain reads the dispatch aloud. A few men look like they want to run.
trivia: On August 24, 1814, British forces under Admiral Cockburn and General Ross burned the Capitol, the President's House, and other government buildings in Washington.
Dolley Madison saved a portrait of George Washington and government documents before fleeing the White House as the British approached.

choices.text: Tell the wavering men you are staying at your post.
choices.result: Two men who were edging toward the tree line come back to the fire. Your captain looks at you once and nods.

choices.text: Say nothing — just check your cartridge box and stay.
choices.result: Quiet steadiness passes through the camp like a current. No speeches needed.

choices.text: Write a quick letter home warning your family to prepare.
choices.result: A dispatch rider takes your letter at a price. The men notice you had ink and paper when they did not.

events.title: The Guns of Fort McHenry
events.text: A squadron of about five bomb ships and a rocket vessel, within a supporting fleet of roughly sixteen to nineteen vessels, opens fire on Fort McHenry. The roar is unlike anything you have heard. Armistead's garrison returns fire. The bombardment lasts through the night and into the next morning.
trivia: The British bombardment of Fort McHenry on September 13–14, 1814 lasted about 25 hours.
Major George Armistead commanded the fort's garrison; a giant American flag was flown over the fort throughout the attack.
Francis Scott Key, held on a British ship during the bombardment, watched the flag and composed 'The Star-Spangled Banner' when he saw it still flying at dawn.
events.leaveText: Hold your position and do nothing more.

attempts.buttonText: Carry ammunition to the forward battery.
attempts.successText: You make the run through shell-fire. The gunners keep loading.
attempts.failureText: A near-miss knocks you flat. You lose a half-day recovering.

attempts.buttonText: Volunteer to hold the embrasure under direct fire.
attempts.successText: You hold the position. The flag stays up. Armistead's men cheer.
attempts.failureText: A bomb-burst throws you back. You survive but cannot stand your post the rest of the night.

events.title: The Road Home
events.text: Word of the Treaty of Ghent has reached camp. The war is over — settled on terms that changed almost no boundary and freed no impressed sailors. Your company is dismissed. The men scatter toward their counties. A neighbor's son — barely seventeen — is sick and cannot make the march alone.
trivia: The Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, ended the War of 1812 with no territorial changes and no formal resolution of impressment.
The Battle of New Orleans was fought after the treaty was signed but before news reached the combatants.

choices.text: Stay back and help him home, however long it takes.
choices.result: Your family waits days longer, not knowing. When you arrive with him, his mother cannot speak. Your own kin look at you with something harder to name.

choices.text: Leave him coin enough to hire a wagon, then go.
choices.result: It costs almost all you have. He makes it home three days after you. No one can quite call it wrong.

choices.text: March home. Your family has waited long enough.
choices.result: You are the first man from your township to walk back through the door. Your family holds you. In town, nobody asks about the boy you left on the road.

events.title: Mid Campaign — The Burning Reaches Your County

text.default: The smoke is visible from the ridge before any messenger arrives. You are thirty miles from home, in federal service, and there is nothing to be done about it. The men from your township say nothing to you directly. They do not have to. You chose this — the larger thing — and the cost of the larger thing is that the smaller thing can burn while you watch from a distance. Whether the position you are defending is worth that calculus is a question nobody here can answer.

You are here, in your own county, when the alarm comes — and that is exactly what you told yourself you would be. You help pull a neighbor's goods from a smoke-filled room. Later, you hear that the federal position held, barely, without your company. You do not know if your presence there would have changed it. You know only that you are standing in the right county, and that this is either the proof you made the right choice or the story you tell yourself about it.

choices.text: Go on.

events.title: Late Campaign — After Fort McHenry, Hearing What the War Settled

text.default: The treaty gives back what was taken and settles almost nothing on paper — no word about impressment, no new borders, no indemnity. Men who crossed state lines and bled for the republic get to hear that the republic fought to a draw. And yet something did settle: you are not the same man who checked a map and asked how far the orders could reach. That question has an answer now, and it lives in you, not in any treaty.

The treaty gives back what was taken and settles almost nothing on paper. Your neighborhood is intact. Your oath was kept in the form you understood it. Whether the war needed you somewhere else — whether a more elastic loyalty would have shortened it or changed it — you will never know. The republic survived without your crossing that line. Whether that means you chose correctly or only that your absence was not decisive is not a question the peace treaty resolves.

sages.name: James Madison
sages.title: President of the United States
sages.bio: James Madison asked Congress to declare war on Britain in June 1812, citing impressment of American sailors, interference with trade, and British support for hostile Indian confederacies. He led the republic through its first constitutional test of war.
sages.greeting: A rider delivers a printed copy of the President's war message to your captain, who reads it aloud. Madison's words list the grievances that brought you here.
sages.advice: The message names three wrongs: sailors seized on the high seas, American trade strangled, and British agents arming tribes on the frontier. Whether the war settles any of them is another question.

choices: British forts still standing on American soil
The impressment of American sailors into the Royal Navy
Spain's refusal to sell Florida

sages.name: Major George Armistead
sages.title: Commander, Fort McHenry
sages.bio: Major George Armistead commanded Fort McHenry during the British naval bombardment of September 1814. His garrison held through a 25-hour bombardment, stopping the British advance on Baltimore and inspiring Francis Scott Key's poem.
sages.greeting: You are assigned a detail near Fort McHenry. Armistead walks the parapet himself, checking the gun positions. He stops and speaks to your squad.
sages.advice: He says the fort will hold because it must — Baltimore is the port that keeps the region alive. He had a flag made large enough that the British could have no difficulty in seeing it from a distance.

question.question: What happened at Fort McHenry on the night of September 13–14, 1814?
choices: American forces surrendered the fort to avoid casualties
British land forces stormed and took the fort
A British naval bombardment failed to capture the fort
The fort was evacuated before the British arrived
question.explanation: The British fleet bombarded Fort McHenry for roughly 25 hours but the garrison held. The British could not silence the fort's guns and abandoned the attack, ending their advance on Baltimore.
question.teksRef: 8.4(B) — Key events and turning points of the War of 1812

sages.name: Francis Scott Key
sages.title: Lawyer and Witness to Fort McHenry
sages.bio: Francis Scott Key was an American lawyer held on a British ship during the bombardment of Fort McHenry. Watching the American flag still flying at dawn, he composed the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner.'
sages.greeting: A lawyer in a dark coat finds your company after the bombardment ends. He says he watched the whole night from a British truce vessel. He seems shaken and lit at the same time.
sages.advice: He says he wrote down what he saw while the words were still in him — the rockets, the bombs, and then the flag still there at first light. He is not sure yet what to do with the lines.

question.question: Where was Francis Scott Key when he wrote the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner'?
choices: On the ramparts of Fort McHenry
In a Baltimore tavern the morning after the battle
Aboard a British truce ship during the bombardment
In Washington watching the Capitol burn
question.explanation: Key had gone to a British ship to negotiate a prisoner's release and was held there during the bombardment. He watched through the night and wrote his poem after seeing the American flag still flying at dawn.

eventTrivia.fact: War Hawks — mostly frontier and southern congressmen like Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun — argued that British interference and frontier provocations demanded war.

eventTrivia.fact: Admiral George Cockburn led the British Chesapeake campaign, including the August 1814 raid that burned Washington's public buildings.

Negotiated a truce with the British commander
Saved a portrait of George Washington and government documents
Fled without taking anything from the White House
eventTrivia.fact: Dolley Madison famously saved a portrait of George Washington and important government documents before evacuating the White House ahead of the British advance in August 1814.

About six hours overnight
About 25 hours through the night and into the next morning
Three full days

eventTrivia.question: What was the outcome of the Treaty of Ghent that ended the War of 1812?
choices: Britain returned Canada to the United States
The United States gained Florida from Spain

Britain agreed to stop all impressment of American sailors

eventTrivia.question: Why did many state militiamen refuse to cross into neighboring states or territories during the war?
choices: They had signed contracts only for two weeks
They believed their constitutional obligation was to defend their own state, not serve as federal troops
Congress had specifically forbidden militia from crossing state lines
They were awaiting pay before agreeing to move
eventTrivia.fact: Many militia members and their officers argued — sincerely and with some constitutional backing — that state militias were raised to defend their own state, not to be pressed into federal service across borders.

choices: The Battle of Lake Erie
The Battle of Queenston Heights
The Battle of New Orleans
The Battle of Plattsburgh

The poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner'
The terms of a prisoner exchange with the British fleet
A newspaper account of Admiral Cockburn's attack
eventTrivia.fact: Watching from a British truce ship, Key wrote the poem 'Defence of Fort McHenry' after seeing the American flag still flying at dawn. It was later set to music and became the national anthem.

eventTrivia.question: What was one major reason American forces struggled in the early years of the war?

The army was well-funded but poorly led

eventTrivia.fact: Congress had severely underfunded the army before the war. State militia systems operated independently and often refused to coordinate, leaving American forces under-supplied and poorly organized in the war's first campaigns.

eventTrivia.question: What did the burning of Washington symbolize for the young republic?
choices: That the United States had secretly allied with France
That the republic's government and national symbols were dangerously vulnerable
That the war had been won by Britain and peace must be made immediately
That state militias were more powerful than the federal army
eventTrivia.fact: The burning of Washington's public buildings in August 1814 — including the Capitol and the President's House — demonstrated how exposed the young republic's institutions were, and became the war's defining humiliation.

eventTrivia.question: What did the successful defense of Fort McHenry accomplish strategically?
choices: It ended the war immediately by forcing British surrender
It stopped the British advance on Baltimore and helped turn the tide of the war
It opened a path for American forces to invade Canada
It destroyed the British fleet in the Chesapeake
eventTrivia.fact: The failure to take Fort McHenry halted the British offensive against Baltimore. Combined with American successes elsewhere, it pushed Britain toward the peace negotiations that produced the Treaty of Ghent.

eventTrivia.question: Which figure commanded Fort McHenry during the British bombardment?
choices: Francis Scott Key
Admiral George Cockburn
Major George Armistead
General William Hull
eventTrivia.fact: Major George Armistead commanded the Fort McHenry garrison through the 25-hour bombardment and refused to surrender, keeping the American flag flying throughout the attack.

eventTrivia.question: Why did War Hawks from western states support the declaration of war in addition to the impressment issue?
choices: They wanted to annex Cuba from Spain
They were angry about British support for Indian resistance on the frontier and restrictions on American trade
They believed the navy was strong enough to defeat Britain at sea
They sought to reopen the Mississippi River to American trade
eventTrivia.fact: Western War Hawks like Henry Clay were furious about British agents supplying and encouraging Indian confederacies resisting American expansion, as well as British trade restrictions that hurt frontier farmers and merchants.

eventTrivia.question: What was the constitutional argument some militia members made for refusing orders to cross state lines?
choices: Only the President, not Congress, could order militia out of state
Militia were raised under state authority to defend their state and could not be constitutionally compelled into federal service beyond that
The Articles of Confederation still governed militia service
The Bill of Rights prohibited the federal government from moving state troops
eventTrivia.fact: The Constitution gave Congress power to call forth militia to repel invasions and suppress insurrections, but many militiamen and governors argued this did not authorize compelling state troops into offensive operations across borders — a dispute that hampered the war effort repeatedly.

eventTrivia.question: What lasting symbol emerged directly from the Battle of Baltimore and the bombardment of Fort McHenry?
choices: The design of the American flag with 50 stars
The national motto 'E Pluribus Unum'
The poem that became the national anthem, 'The Star-Spangled Banner'
The tradition of flying the flag at half-staff on war memorials
eventTrivia.fact: Francis Scott Key's poem, written while watching the bombardment from a British ship, became 'The Star-Spangled Banner' — eventually the national anthem — making Fort McHenry the birthplace of one of America's most enduring national symbols.

data.historicalContext: The War of 1812 ended in December 1814 with the Treaty of Ghent, which restored pre-war boundaries and resolved none of the stated causes — impressment was not abolished, no territory changed hands. The Battle of New Orleans was fought weeks after the treaty was signed. The war left the United States with a sense of national identity hardened by survival, a burned capital, a national anthem, and the same unresolved tensions that had started it. State militias had proven unreliable; the regular army's weakness had nearly cost the republic its capital. The republic endured — but not because it was ready.

verdict.good: You held your post when it cost something to hold it. You shared what you had when you had little, you spoke for the men when it would have been easier to stay quiet, and you stayed beside a sick neighbor on the road home when your own family was waiting. The war ended with no impressed sailor freed, no boundary moved, no cause settled. The republic survived by luck and stubbornness as much as virtue. You were part of what held. That is not nothing — and in 1814, it was most of what there was.
verdict.bad: You did the math every time, and the math always came out in your favor. You kept your coins when a hungry man sat by your fire. You told a politician what he wanted to hear for a coin in your palm. You marched home first and let a sick boy find his own way. The war ended with nothing settled and the capital's ashes still cooling. You came back fed and paid and slightly ahead. The men who stood in the rain at Fort McHenry all night stood there without you — or with a version of you that was already counting the walk home.
verdict.indifferent: You moved through the war without it ever really touching you. When choices came you took the one that asked the least, waited for someone else to act, and kept your head down until the noise passed. The capital burned, Fort McHenry held, and a lawyer on a British ship wrote down words that would outlast everyone in your company. You were there for all of it and nowhere in it. The treaty changed nothing and neither did you. History did not record where you stood. You were not sure you could say either.

data.reviewSummary:
The War of 1812 began with a list of grievances that had been building for years. The most urgent was impressment — the Royal Navy's practice of stopping American ships and seizing sailors it deemed British subjects, forcing thousands of Americans into British naval service against their will. Added to this were British trade restrictions that strangled American commerce and, on the western frontier, evidence that British agents were supplying and encouraging Indian confederacies resisting American expansion. War Hawks in Congress — frontier and southern representatives like Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun — pushed President James Madison to act. In June 1812, Madison asked Congress to declare war, and it did.

The early years went badly. Congress had underfunded the army and the state militia systems were fragmented and unreliable; many militia members refused orders to cross state lines, arguing their constitutional obligation extended only to defending their own state. American forces failed repeatedly in attempts to invade Canada.

The war's lowest point came in August 1814, when British forces under Admiral George Cockburn marched into Washington and burned the Capitol and the President's House. Dolley Madison, before evacuating, saved a portrait of George Washington and important government documents. The young republic's institutions had never looked more exposed.

The tide turned at Baltimore. On the night of September 13–14, 1814, a British fleet bombarded Fort McHenry for roughly 25 hours. Major George Armistead commanded the garrison and refused to surrender, keeping the American flag flying throughout. The British could not silence the fort's guns and abandoned the attack. An American lawyer, Francis Scott Key, had been held on a British truce ship during the entire bombardment; seeing the flag still there at dawn, he wrote the poem that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner' — eventually the national anthem.

The war ended with the Treaty of Ghent, signed December 24, 1814, which restored pre-war boundaries and formally resolved nothing — impressment was not abolished, no territory changed hands. The Battle of New Orleans was fought weeks later, before news of peace arrived. The republic had survived, but the causes it went to war over remained unsettled.
